title: Letter 15 — The Spectacle of the Whole World
attribution_note: Letter 15 of 46 in the collection Letters Sent — see Letter 1 for provenance.

pairs.en: Long have I not written to you. Forgive me; I am to blame. Now I write, and in this picture, as far as I am able, I set before you the spectacle of the whole world. Look upon it and take heed, and consider concerning yourself how you contend, lest you repent later, when it is late and of no use.

Our life in this age is nothing other than a path to the age to come. Upon this path we step at the time of birth, and at the time of death we finish it. And every one who lives upon the earth is a wayfarer. This path for some is very short, as for infants who die; for others it is longer, as for children and young men who die; for others longer still, as for men and old men who die. As the day and the manner of the beginning of this path are known to us — for we are all alike born — so the day, the hour, and the manner of its ending are unknown, for we know not how or when we shall finish it. Take heed of this! The end will overtake us there where we look not for it, and then it overtakes us when we hope not. Consider and remember this. Blessed and wise is he who considers and remembers this.

Therefore be always upon the path such as you wish to be at the end, and you will be blessed! Guard against sin, and repent of sins already committed, as men at their end guard against sin and repent. Consider riches, honour, glory, pleasures, and the other things of this world upon the path as men consider them at the end. Pray to God upon the path, call upon Him, and seek mercy of Him, as men pray at the end, and you will be blessed. Then, wherever the end overtakes you, and however it overtakes you, and whenever it overtakes you, you will make a blessed end.

If our life upon the earth is a path, and we are wayfarers, *“strangers and pilgrims, as were all our fathers”* [1 Chronicles 29:15; Hebrews 11:13; Psalm 38:13], then our Fatherland, our home, our place of rest, our inheritance is not here — otherwise we should always have to remain here without departing. Why, then, do we hide our treasures upon the path? Why upon the path and in our sojourning do we seek honour, glory, and comforts? Why do we receive this world as our Fatherland? For we are not born and enter the world for the sake of treasure, riches, honour, glory, and the other comforts, but for this: that we may pass over into that age; since as we entered this world, so we must also go out of it; and as we brought nothing into the world, so we shall carry nothing out.

*“For we brought nothing into this world, and it is certain we can carry nothing out,”* teaches the apostle [1 Timothy 6:7]. And the very fact shows this. For neither the rich man carries out his riches, nor the man of rank his honour, nor the well-born his nobility, nor the famous his glory, nor any of the rest. The end makes all equal. For where the master lies in the earth, where his servant, where the man of rank, where the lowly, where the rich, where the poor — it is impossible to know. Therefore it is written: *“He heapeth up riches, and knoweth not who shall gather them”* [Psalm 38:7]. *“They shall leave their wealth to others.* *When he dieth he shall carry nothing away: his glory shall not descend after him”* [Psalm 48:11, 18].

You see that from the wayfarer at his end everything departs, and as he himself entered the world naked, so naked he goes out of the world — and would that it were only naked, and not drunken with the love of the world, which *“is enmity with God”* [James 4:4; 1 John 2:15], and not burdened with sins! Therefore the glory of this world, honour and riches and the other comforts, are as a shadow, as a dream, as a vapour, *“that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away”* [James 4:14], and turns to nothing. Why, then, chase after a shadow, a dream, and a vapour, and leave the truth? Why seek what today or tomorrow must be left behind?

sections.heading: Need and the lust for more

pairs.en: They will say: “I seek that I may have wherewith to be fed.”

Answer. This is not forbidden; one must labour and seek wherewith to be fed, but justly. Yet to gather and to grow rich in this world is forbidden to Christians [see Luke 12:15–31]. Moreover, nature is content with little: it requires only what is needful; *“having food and raiment, let us be therewith content”* [1 Timothy 6:8]. Lust needs much; it is not content with what it has, but desires more and more, like one who has a fever within, who always thirsts and cannot drink enough.

See whether under the guise of need you are not serving mammon, and whether, where food is proposed, the love of money does not hide. Lust is crafty and deceitful; it invents much for its own sake, and always, under the guise of food, schemes poison for the soul.

Remember that you are a wayfarer. And honour, rank, glory, the praise of men, which the sons of this age desire no less than riches — for what are they needful, to what end are they required? What profit is there from them? The body does not require them; life is preserved without them, for many live without glory, honour, praise, or rank. The soul will go into that age without all of that. What necessity here can a man present who desires and seeks these things? What remains to be said and confessed, if not that *“all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world”* [1 John 2:16]?

You see that the desire of riches, honour, glory, and the rest is a burden which weighs down wayfarers and bows them to the earth, and does not permit them, as men, to look toward heaven, for which all were created and by holy Baptism renewed. O how many this heavy burden has weighed down and plunged into the abyss! See, consider, and beware.

Who hides treasure in a foreign country? Does he not send it to his Fatherland? Who burdens himself upon the path? Does he not rather cast the load from himself? Who in captivity and exile seeks to be glorified? Does he not rather sigh toward his Fatherland and desire liberation?

You are a stranger upon the earth and a sojourner; why, then, do you hide your treasure here? You are a wayfarer; why do you burden yourself? You are in captivity and exile, cast out of paradise; why do you seek glory here? Why do you not sigh toward the Fatherland you have lost, and seek not its glory, where there is honour, riches, and eternal glory, as also eternal life? It is plain that you take a foreign country for your Fatherland and the path for a home, if you seek much here.

Woe to those who have a foreign country as Fatherland and the path as a home! For *“where their treasure is, there will their heart be also”* [Matthew 6:21]. *“For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul”* [Matthew 16:26]? What profit is there to a man if he find the temporal, of which he will soon be deprived, and be deprived of the eternal, which, once found, will never be lost?

The human soul is like a mirror. In a mirror, when it is turned toward heaven, heaven is depicted; and when toward the earth, the earth is depicted: so also in the soul is depicted that which it loves and of which it thinks. Does it love this world and the things that are in the world — glory, honour, praise, riches, pleasure? — these are depicted in it. Does it love God and the heavenly kingdom? — these are depicted in it.

And what the soul loves, that it seeks, for that it cares, of that it thinks. So *“where”* a man's beloved *“treasure”* is, *“there will his heart be also.”* And what the soul loved while living in this world, what it sought, that will appear with it, depicted in it, in that age. So a man's deeds, words, and thoughts follow him into that age, and will appear at Christ's Judgment before all the Angels and men and before God the Judge Himself; and the man himself will then see what he did, loved, sought, for what he cared, and of what he thought in the world. The soul must return to God again naked of sin and of the love of this world, as it came forth from God naked. Consider diligently and mark this, O soul that would be saved! Behold the path set before you in general!
The path of this present life is twofold: the narrow and the broad.

The way is narrow because the wayfarers who go by it are surrounded by temptations, troubles, calamities, and sorrows, which must be endured; and they take captive their own will, constrain it, bow it, and subject it to the will of their Creator and God. By this way go the godly, the God-fearing, and the faithful servants of Christ, who have given Him their names with their hearts, and who *“crucify the flesh with the affections and lusts”* [Galatians 5:24]; and each bears his own cross, laid upon him by God the heavenly Father; and they follow Christ, the Son of God, their Lord, who bore the Cross for us all and was crucified upon the Cross — and He leads them into the heavenly Fatherland.

Jesus the son of Nun brought the sons of Israel into the promised land, as we read in the holy Bible; and Jesus the Son of God, who appeared upon the earth in the flesh and suffered and rose from the dead, brings His faithful into heaven — the land *“flowing with milk and honey”* [Exodus 33:3] of eternal sweetness and comfort. Mark well here that Jesus brings into heaven those who follow Him, and not those who do not follow.

The broad way is so called because its wayfarers live according to their own will, do what they wish, look not to the will of their Creator and God, bow not their will under the yoke of Christ, but enlarge the will of their hearts; they have cast off the cross and loved this age, and bear upon their shoulders the yoke of Satan, burdened with sins and iniquities. Here belong the lovers of pleasure, the lovers of luxury, the takers of bribes, the extortioners, those who serve mammon and not God, fornicators, adulterers, plunderers, thieves, drunkards, those who hate their neighbours, the malicious and the vengeful, slanderers, evil-speakers, mockers, the false and flatterers, the foul-mouthed, lovers of foolish talk, blasphemers, the stingy, the unmerciful, card-players — especially those who play for money — and all who work unrighteousness and fear not God, and tremble not before His words; for all such live in the breadth of their own desires.

Enter not, O my soul, into their counsel. *“Fret not thyself because of evildoers, neither be thou envious against the workers of iniquity.* *For they shall soon be cut down like the grass, and wither as the green herb.* *Rest in the Lord, and wait patiently for Him.* *Fret not thyself because of him who prospereth in his way, because of the man who bringeth wicked devices to pass.* *For yet a little while, and the wicked shall not be: yea, thou shalt diligently consider his place, and it shall not be.* *But the transgressors shall be destroyed together: the end of the wicked shall be cut off.* *The righteous shall inherit the land, and dwell therein for ever.* *Wait on the Lord, and keep His way, and He shall exalt thee to inherit the land: when the wicked are cut off, thou shalt see it”* [Psalm 36:1–2, 7, 10, 28–29, 34]. *“Wait on the Lord: be of good courage, and He shall strengthen thine heart: wait, I say, on the Lord”* [Psalm 26:14]. Let *“the law of Thy mouth”* be to thee *“better unto me than thousands of gold and silver”* [Psalm 118:72]. *“Truly my soul waiteth upon God: from Him cometh my salvation.* *He only is my rock and my salvation;* *He is my defence”* [Psalm 61:2–3].

The way of the ungodly is broad, but it leads into the straitness of eternal torments. Look concerning this in the Holy Scripture, which is *“a lamp unto our feet,”* at the places set down below [Psalm 49:17–22; 51:3–9; 1 Corinthians 6:9–10; Galatians 5:20–21; Matthew 25:41–46; Revelation 21:8; John 3:14–15; Matthew 6:15; 7:23; 8:12; 18:23–25; Ephesians 5:5; Isaiah 1 and the rest], which all show that an unlawful and spacious life leads to eternal perdition. The cause of this is that such people resist the will of God, which *“will have all men to be saved”*; and they will not truly repent, which the will of God desires, but follow the will of their own hearts. And the Lord says plainly: *“And he that taketh not his cross, and followeth after Me, is not worthy of Me”* [Matthew 10:38]. And if he is not worthy of Christ, of whom is he worthy if not of His adversary, whose will he follows?

sections.heading: Enter ye in at the strait gate

pairs.en: Therefore the Lord says: *“Enter ye in at the strait gate: for wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat: because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it”* [Matthew 7:13–14].

Why do many walk the broad way? Because each wishes to live in the breadth of his own will and desires. Why do few find the narrow way? Because few wish to humble themselves, to take captive their own will and subject it to the will of God, and to endure what the narrow way requires.

Why does the narrow way *“lead unto life”*? Because those who walk this way truly repent, humble themselves, fear God, endure, and follow Christ in humility, patience, love, and the other virtues. For Christ brings into life only those who follow Him, and not those who turn aside from Him.

Why does *“the broad way lead to destruction”*? Because those who walk it resist the will of God; they will not humble themselves, truly repent, cease from a sinful life, and hate what the will of God hates. Therefore the Lord says: *“Not every one that saith unto Me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of My Father which is in heaven”* [Matthew 7:21]. And again: *“And why call ye Me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say”* [Luke 6:46]?

sections.heading: The spectacle of the whole world

pairs.en: Behold for you the universal spectacle! You see those who complete the course, but not alike, and each presses toward his own centre. Honours and crowns are received only by those who go by the narrow and sorrowful, the cross-bearing and Christian way [see 2 Timothy 2:12; James 1:12]. The apostle of Christ bids us so run that we may obtain: *“So run, that ye may obtain”* [1 Corinthians 9:24]. Upon this spectacle it is not an earthly king and the sons of this age who look, but the King of heaven with His elect, the Angels and all the saints, looking down from heaven [Psalm 10:4–5; 32:13, 15; 13:2; 2 Chronicles 16:9; Zechariah 9:1; Jeremiah 32:19; 16:17]. The King of heaven looks, and praises only those who go by the way of His commandments and of patience, who bear His good yoke; and He prepares for them crowns not fading but unfading, and honours not temporal but eternal; and from the spacious way He calls all away, and invites them to the narrow way. *“Come unto Me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.* *Take My yoke upon you, and learn of Me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls.* *For My yoke is easy, and My burden is light”* [Matthew 11:28–30].

Let us hearken, O Christians, to the heavenly King while He calls — to Him whom we must without fail obey. For if we hearken to an earthly king and fulfil all that he commands, that we may not be deprived of his mercy and fall under his wrath, then how much more must we hearken to the King of heaven, God, to be deprived of whose mercy is plain perdition, and whose wrath delivers to eternal punishment. And turning aside from the pernicious breadth, let us enter upon the saving straitness, that by this straitness we may enter into the breadth of eternal comforts.

O, it is time, it is time: *“It is time for Thee, Lord, to work”* [Psalm 118:126]! Behold, the path is shortened; behold, the end is near; we have come nearer to the end today than yesterday, and we know not when we shall finish it. Behold, *“He that shall come will come, and will not tarry,”* and *“shall reward every man according to his works”* [Hebrews 10:36; Matthew 16:27]. Behold, the Archangel's trumpet will soon sound; behold, soon *“the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God: and they that hear shall live,”* and *“we shall all be changed”* [John 5:25, 28; 1 Corinthians 15:51]. Behold, soon *“the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night,”* behold, *“the heavens shall pass away with a great noise, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat, the earth also and the works that are therein shall be burned up”* [2 Peter 3:10]. *“Behold, I come quickly; and My reward is with Me, to give every man according as his work shall be”* [Revelation 22:7, 12].

Watch and pray, O my soul, *“for ye know neither the day nor the hour wherein the Son of man cometh”* [Matthew 25:13]. Then from the face of the fear of the coming Judge the whole world will tremble. Then kings and princes, the mighty and the glorious, the rich and all who in this world count themselves something great, who here enlarged themselves in the desires of their hearts, will wish to hide themselves in caves and in the rocks. Remember this, O man, and stand upon the way of Christ, and be established. Let that voice always ring in the ears of your soul: “Arise, ye dead, and go to the Judgment!” *“Teach me Thy way, O Lord: quicken me in Thy way”* [Psalm 85:11; 118:37].

sections.heading: Better to suffer here than there

pairs.en: Believe, O Christian, the word of God. It is true, it is trustworthy; it can in no wise lie, for it is the word of the true and righteous God. It, as a lamp, shows us what is pernicious and what is saving. It declares with certainty that the broad way leads to perdition, and the narrow leads to life; for the spacious way is Satan's, and the narrow way is Christ's. Therefore it is better by the narrow way of patience and the lowly way of humility to go into life, than by the spacious way of desires and the high way of pride to go into perdition. Better to endure all things temporally, than there to endure without end.

If it were permitted to the souls that have departed and are tormented in hell to return into this world, then they would — I speak without doubt — desire with eagerness, joy, and thanksgiving to pass through every straitness and sorrow, and for many years, if only they might be delivered from that calamity. The rich would desire to be in the uttermost poverty, and to endure all things. The lovers of pleasure would desire to feed on roots and greens and water, and that in measure, and to endure all things. The lovers of glory would desire to be in extreme contempt, dishonour, and reproach, and to endure all things. Princes, nobles, and masters would desire to be slaves to their own servants, whom they held for the dust under their feet, if not worse, and to serve them.

In a word, every sinner who is there would desire to endure all things here. But this will be given to none. They heard the word of God here, and believed not; they were exhorted, and hearkened not; they were corrected, and amended not; they were called to repentance, and repented not. They repent now, but late and without profit, and they will repent for ever. They hear the word: *“Son, remember that thou in thy lifetime receivedst thy good things”* [Luke 16:25].

The same will befall those who now walk the spacious way. Therefore it is better with Lazarus, who suffered here, to suffer temporally, and there to rest eternally in Abraham's bosom, than with the rich man, who made merry here, to make merry temporally, and there to suffer in the flame eternally [see Luke 16:19–31]. Better to humble oneself here and be exalted there, than to be exalted here and be humbled there. *“For every one that exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted”* [Luke 18:14].

Better to weep for sins here, where weeping is profitable, and to be comforted there, than to take comfort in the flesh here, and to weep there, where weeping is of no use. *“Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted”* [Matthew 5:4]. Better here to endure persecution, reproach, mockery, affliction, every suffering, and there to have a portion with the martyrs, than here to persecute, afflict, mock, and torment, and there to suffer with the tormentors. For here all is temporal, short, soon-passing, and light; but there eternal, unceasing, and heavy.

Choose, O my soul, the better; choose the light and the short, that you may escape the heavy and the unceasing, and receive instead of temporal sorrow eternal comfort, instead of temporal dishonour eternal glory, instead of temporal calamity eternal blessedness. For one must either endure here, or there — without fail. One must either go by the narrow way, and go into life, or go by the spacious, and go into perdition: one of the two is set before every one who lives upon the earth to choose.

A change will meet all who live upon the face of the earth; to every one his own lot will fall. *“It is a righteous thing with God”* to *“recompense”* what is due *“to them that trouble you, and to you who are troubled”* [2 Thessalonians 1:6–10] — to God, who *“shall reward every man according to his works”* [Matthew 16:27]: to them who by patient continuance in well doing seek for glory and honour and immortality, eternal life; but unto them that are contentious, and do not obey the truth, but obey unrighteousness, indignation and wrath. *“Tribulation and anguish, upon every soul of man that doeth evil,”* and the rest [Romans 2:6–9].

The proud will be humbled, and the humble exalted. The mouths of the mockers will be stopped, and they will be silent, and shame will cover them; and those who were mocked will stand with boldness and lift up their heads. Those who offend will be in sorrow, and those who were offended will receive comfort. The rich and the full will be made poor and hunger, and the poor will be enriched, and the hungry filled; and *“they that seek the Lord shall not want any good thing”* [Psalm 33:11]. Those who cast out will be rejected, and those who were cast out will be received. Those who laugh and rejoice with this world will weep, and those who mourn will be comforted. Those who glorify themselves will be abased, and those who abase themselves will be glorified. Those who make merry will thirst and desire a drop of water each day, and *“they shall be abundantly satisfied with the fatness of Thy house; and Thou shalt make them drink of the river of Thy pleasures”* [Psalm 35:9] — those who fear God and serve Him.

To each will be his own. *“God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap”* [Galatians 6:7]. *“And these”* (the sinners) *“shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal”* [Matthew 25:46]. Then will begin eternity without end. Some in heaven, in their longed-for Fatherland, will without end, after the labours, sorrows, and calamities received here for the sake of godliness, rest, rejoice, make merry, be comforted, and reign with Christ the King; and others in hell will likewise without end suffer and be tormented with the devil and his angels.

Blessed and wise is he who here, in this world, lives as a wayfarer, as a stranger and a sojourner, and, *“having here no continuing city, seeks one to come, whose builder and maker is God”* [Hebrews 13:14; 11:10]. Blessed is he who turns his eyes away from time and the temporal and turns them to eternity and the eternal — truly blessed! For such a one will not seek upon the path riches, glory, honours, comfort, and be weighed down by these as by a burden (for what need has he of all that which sooner or later he will leave upon the path?), but will always lift the eyes of his heart toward his desired Fatherland and city, as a stranger toward his home, as a wayfarer toward his goal, as one cast out and captive toward his Fatherland, as one far away toward his father, as one who labours toward his rest, as one in calamity toward his blessedness, as one sitting in prison toward his freedom, as a contender toward his honour and glory. *“For where his treasure is, there will his heart be also”* [Matthew 6:21]. Thither he will send his desires, his sighings, and his wares that are fit for this. Choose and hold fast, O my soul, this blessedness.

Foolish and wretched is he who in this world, upon this path, in this exile, captivity, and sojourning, lives as in a Fatherland, rests, takes comfort, delights himself, and is not careful that, living in time, he forgets eternity, and, leaving heaven, turns to the earth and the earthly as a beast, and seeks only what the senses see and with which they take comfort. *“Turn away mine eyes from beholding vanity”* [Psalm 118:37].
*“Blessed is that man that maketh the Lord his trust, and respecteth not the proud, nor such as turn aside to lies”* [Psalm 39:5].

Whoever wishes to leave the spacious path and stand upon the Christian way (and this every one who wishes to be saved must do) must leave off evil works and turn to God with repentance and with sorrow that he lived in the breadth of his own will and despised the will of God, and must change himself and begin a new life pleasing to God. Upon the Christian way, at the very beginning, it is required that the man who wishes to go by it deny himself; for so the Lord teaches: *“Whosoever will come after Me, let him deny himself”* [Mark 8:34].
What does it mean, *“to deny himself”*?

Answer. To become other than he was before — not according to nature, but according to the inner state: for the lover of money, to renounce the love of money; for the lover of glory, the love of glory; for the fornicator and the adulterer, unclean lust; for the wrathful and the malicious, wrath and malice; for the proud, pride; for the unmerciful, his hard-heartedness; in a word, for the man of evil manners, to renounce his evil manners. So nature will be the same, but manners will be other. What God created will be the same, but what man himself has made will be changed; and so the man will be other — other in manners, but the same in nature.

It is related that a certain young man lived impurely with a harlot, and, wishing to leave off that foul work and amend himself, withdrew from her for a time. And when he felt that the lust for her had been quenched in him, he returned home and, meeting her by chance, passed by in silence. And when on another day he met her again and, saying nothing to her, went past, she said to him: “Why, I am such-and-such. How did you not know me?” “But I am not the same,” he answered.

So be you also not the same that you were before. Change yourself, and you will not be the same. Seek not the glory, honour, riches, and pleasure of this world; be not angry and avenge not when they revile and wrong you; delight not, take not pleasure, take not comfort, and exalt not yourself when they praise you; grieve not and murmur not over property stolen from you, and the rest — and you will not be the same. And this is what it is *“to deny himself.”* Then you will go by the narrow way and bear your cross, and will follow Christ.

sections.heading: The heart and the outer life

pairs.en: When a man renounces his evil manners and amends his inner state, then his outer works, words, and undertakings will also be sound: the hands will not do what is evil, the tongue will not speak what is evil, the feet will not go to what is evil, the ears will not hear, the eyes will not look upon what is evil, since the will will not desire what is evil, but only what is good; and so there will be a good agreement between the heart, or the inner state, and the outer members and their doings. For from the heart every work and word depends: from a righteous and good heart a righteous and good work and word comes. So from a pure well pure streams flow. So good psalteries give forth a good sound. So a good bell rings well. So a vessel with sweet spices gives forth a good and pleasant smell. So, according to the word of the Lord, *“every good tree bringeth forth good fruit”* [Matthew 7:17].

Temptation follows upon true virtue. Satan always rises up against the servants of Christ, and by God's permission, now through himself, now through evil men, works them evil. Here every godly man needs patience, and must bear without murmuring and with magnanimity all that is contrary that may befall him, and overcome by patience, and receive all this that befalls him as sent from God, that he may show that he honours God not in pretence. So Satan is put to shame, and the man who truly honours God is made known and is crowned.

So the temptation that came upon holy Job from the devil, which he bore with magnanimity, showed that he was a true worshipper of God. And the devil found nothing more with which to accuse him — he who before had accused and said: *“Doth Job fear God for nought”* [Job 1:9]? And so, overcome and put to shame by his patience, he was silent.

And this is what it is *“to take up his cross”* — that is, to be ready to endure all that is contrary that may befall, even unto death itself, if this be needful for God's sake. What does it mean *“to bear his cross”*? Answer: to endure without murmuring and with magnanimity all that may befall.

sections.heading: Take up the cross and follow

pairs.en: So he who bears his cross must follow Christ, as the Lord said: *“and take up his cross, and follow Me”* [Mark 8:34].
What does it mean *“to follow Christ”*?

Answer. Many bear their cross, but do not follow Christ. Such are those who do evil works and suffer — as, for example, malefactors, thieves, robbers, murderers, plunderers, fornicators, drunkards, and the rest. They bear a cross — that is, they endure either reproach, or beating, or bonds, or exile, or death itself — but they do not follow Christ.
What, then, does it mean *“to follow Christ”*?

Answer. To do good, and to endure every calamity for the sake of the will of God, which desires our patience, looking unto Christ Himself, who so suffered. Christ did all things righteously, *“and did no sin”* [1 Peter 2:22], and taught what is good, but every calamity and misfortune He endured and suffered for our sake, *“doing the will of Him that sent Him”* the Father [John 4:34], *“and finishing His work,”* and was *“obedient unto death, even the death of the cross”* [John 4:34; Philippians 2:8].

So by His example He has taught us how we ought to please God — that is, to do good and to endure calamity, that so we may do the will of God. For the will of God desires that we do good and bear with magnanimity all that is contrary that befalls from Satan or from evil men, and overcome by patience.

*“Christ also suffered for us, leaving us an example, that ye should follow His steps.”* And this is the apostolic teaching: *“For this is thankworthy, if a man for conscience toward God endure grief, suffering wrongfully.* *For what glory is it, if, when ye be buffeted for your faults, ye shall take it patiently? but if, when ye do well, and suffer for it, ye take it patiently, this is acceptable with God.* *For even hereunto were ye called”* [1 Peter 2:19–21].

Therefore if any one does good and suffers unjustly, and endures for the love of God and of Christ the Son of God — that is, because Christ for the love of His heavenly Father and for the love of us, the unworthy, so suffered and endured — that man follows Christ in humility, patience, and love, and bears his cross, and goes by the narrow and Christian way, and goes into the eternal kingdom, as He says: *“If any man serve Me, let him follow Me; and where I am, there shall also My servant be”* [John 12:26].
So you see what the narrow way is. From this understand that *“few there be that find it”* [Matthew 7:14].

You see what it means *“to deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow Christ.”* Know that few deny themselves and follow Christ. All wish to be glorified with Christ, but few wish to be with Him who suffers. But Christ says: *“And he that taketh not his cross, and followeth after Me, is not worthy of Me”* [Matthew 10:38]. And again: *“Whosoever therefore shall be ashamed of Me and of My words in this adulterous and sinful generation; of him also shall the Son of man be ashamed, when He cometh in the glory of His Father with the holy angels”* [Mark 8:38]. And again: *“In your patience possess ye your souls”* [Luke 21:19]. And in the Acts of the Apostles it is written: *“we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God”* [Acts 14:22]. See: not only through tribulations, but through many tribulations do men enter into the kingdom of God.

sections.heading: It is not unbearable to endure

pairs.en: They will say: “It is heavy and unbearable for me to endure.”

Answer. Heavier it will be to hear: *“I know you not whence ye are”* [Luke 13:25]; *“Depart from Me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire”* [Matthew 25:41]. It is not unbearable to endure — you simply will not endure. To him who wills, with God's help, all things are possible. God helps him who truly and in deed wills what He Himself commands: He commands to endure, and helps to endure [see 2 Corinthians 6:2; Hebrews 4:16; 13:5–6].

What will not those who love do for the sake of their beloved? How do they not suffer, that they may please them? What troubles will not the lovers of glory undergo, to obtain vain glory? What calamities will not merchants endure, to gather temporal riches? To what danger will not soldiers expose themselves, to please an earthly king and obtain rank?

And is it unbearable for you to endure for the sake of your God, and so to please Him, and to obtain from Him the promised eternal glory — from Him who both commands you to endure and wills to help you in your endurance? Moreover, God suffers us not to be tempted above our strength. Upon a crystal or glass vessel the craftsman strikes lightly, that it may not be broken, but upon silver and copper he strikes hard: so to the weak a light temptation is permitted, and to the strong a heavier. *“God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able,”* — so the apostle of Christ teaches and comforts the faithful [1 Corinthians 10:13]. Therefore we must shut our mouths and endure in silence all that may befall, and receive it as from the hand of the Lord.

Consider, O Christian, how much Christ our King and Lord suffered for our sake, and what He endured — for our sake, I say, His unprofitable servants, that He might *“seek and to save that which was lost”* [Matthew 18:11]! Read the Gospel, and you will see. Does not justice require that we also, His servants, for His sake, our King and Lord, endure all things, and so gratefully repay Him love for His love? For love is repaid by nothing other than love, which is known in nothing so much as in enduring for the beloved.
Upon the narrow way and in the bearing of the cross one must pray with zeal, that God Himself may help in endurance. *“For without Me ye can do nothing”* [John 15:5].
Be saved.
